newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: After 200 years, Australia to consider republic.
newsitem.headline: After 200 years, Australia to consider republic.

text.p: Australia's government on Tuesday said it would hold a national convention this year to consider how to become a republic, a move that would sever more than 200 years of constitutional ties with former colonial power Britain.

Prime Minister John Howard told parliament the constitutional convention would be held in November or December to consider how Australia can become a republic, replacing Britain's Queen Elizabeth with an Australian head-of-state.
The Australian Republican Movement welcomed the move, but expressed some concerns about the convention, preferring to go direct to a national vote on the republic.
Opinion polls show about half of Australian voters want a republic, but also that they think the country faces more pressing problems. Many are uncommitted.

Howard said his Liberal-National government would appoint half the convention's delegates, including several Aborigines and young Australians aged between 18 and 25. The other half would be chosen by voters in a voluntary postal ballot.
The plan was endorsed by government parliamentarians earlier on Tuesday during their first meeting for the year.

But Howard, who made a 1996 election pledge to hold a convention, declared his strong support for Australia's constitutional monarchy, saying he did not believe a republic would be as stable or effective.
"As members of the parliament will know, I am certainly not Australia's leading republican," Howard said.
"I do not believe that any republican system of government can deliver more stable or more effective government than can the present constitution," he said.
Former Labor prime minister Paul Keating, ousted by Howard last year, ignited the republican push in 1995.
Howard acknowledged a strong desire for change among some Australians, appealing to monarchists and republicans not to allow the issue to split the community.
"It is very important that this issue not be allowed to create unnecessary divisions in the Australian community."
Howard did not say when a national vote on becoming a republic would be held, adding Australia's economic problems were more important.
But government sources have said if the convention was held this year, a final national vote on a republic could be held before or with the next election, due in early 1999.
The A$50 million (US$38 million) convention will produce options for a republic to be voted on in a national plebiscite, but this vote would not be binding on the government.
The result of the plebiscite would form the basis of a national referendum, which would have to be passed by a majority of voters in a majority of Australia's six states.

The Australian Republican Movement (ARM) said it believed all the delegates to the convention should be elected and that the government could be accused of stacking the convention if it appointed half the delegates.
ARM chairman Malcolm Turnbull said republicans would prefer to go straight to a national vote on the matter.
"You could be excused for saying the government is going a very long way round doing something that could be done very simply," Turnbull told a news conference in Sydney.
